latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Aging arterial walls, especially extracranial branches of the carotid and aortic branches, develop permissive adventitial dendritic-cell activation with impaired immune checkpoint control. This creates the host substrate for giant cell arteritis rather than a generic large-vessel vasculitis state.
IL-6, IL-1, TNF, Th1, and Th17 activity drive fever, malaise, anemia of inflammation, thrombocytosis, high ESR/CRP, and steroid-responsive systemic symptoms.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Granulomatous medium- and large-artery wall inflammation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: CD4 T cells, macrophages, multinucleated giant cells, matrix metalloproteinases, and reactive oxygen species attack elastic lamina and media in susceptible arteries.

Inflammation of superficial temporal, occipital, maxillary, facial, lingual, and other external carotid branches produces new headache, scalp tenderness, tender or pulseless temporal arteries, and craniofacial pain.
Luminal narrowing in maxillary, facial, lingual, and temporal arterial branches produces jaw claudication, tongue claudication, scalp ischemic pain, and chewing-induced craniofacial fatigue.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Ophthalmic and posterior ciliary artery ischemia
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Arteritis and occlusive remodeling in ophthalmic, posterior ciliary, retinal, or vertebrobasilar branches causes amaurosis fugax, diplopia, anterior or posterior ischemic optic neuropathy, retinal artery occlusion, and irreversible vision loss.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Aortitis and extracranial large-vessel branch inflammation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: GCA can involve the aorta, subclavian, axillary, carotid, vertebral, iliac, femoral, and other branches, often with constitutional symptoms, limb claudication, bruits, pulse deficits, or imaging-detected wall inflammation.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Intimal hyperplasia with stenosis and occlusion
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Macrophage-derived growth factors and smooth-muscle migration produce concentric intimal hyperplasia, arterial stenosis, occlusion, tissue ischemia, and persistent symptoms after inflammatory activity falls.
Shared inflammatory biology with polymyalgia rheumatica produces shoulder and hip girdle pain, prolonged morning stiffness, bursitis, tenosynovitis, and systemic inflammatory symptoms.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Aortic elastic lamina destruction and aneurysm remodeling
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Chronic granulomatous aortitis weakens the aortic media and elastic lamina, producing delayed thoracic or abdominal aneurysm, dissection, and aortic regurgitation risk even after cranial symptoms improve.
Residual vessel-wall immune niches and remodeled stenotic segments create relapse risk during glucocorticoid taper and persistent ischemic symptoms despite normalized inflammatory markers.

High-dose glucocorticoids, IL-6 receptor blockade, and other steroid-sparing immunosuppressants increase serious infection, viral reactivation, metabolic toxicity, bone loss, and treatment-limiting adverse-event hazards.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Adventitial dendritic-cell activation and age-related immune dysregulation permit systemic Th1/Th17/IL-6 inflammation.
Th1, Th17, IL-6, TNF, and macrophage activation recruit and maintain granulomatous arteritis in susceptible vessels.
The cranial phenotype reflects the same granulomatous arteritis concentrated in superficial temporal and other external carotid branches.
Extracranial large-vessel GCA is granulomatous arteritis in the aorta and major branches rather than a separate first-layer disease.
Macrophage and smooth-muscle activation drive intimal hyperplasia, stenosis, and occlusion downstream of active arteritis.
Inflamed external carotid branches develop ischemia during chewing and scalp perfusion demand.
Cranial branch involvement can extend to ophthalmic and posterior ciliary circulation, causing transient or permanent ocular ischemia.
Large-vessel wall inflammation heals with fibrotic stenosis, occlusion, or persistent arterial remodeling.
Chronic aortitis damages the media and elastic lamina, producing delayed aneurysm or dissection risk.
Relapsing vessel-wall immune activity reactivates systemic inflammatory markers and constitutional symptoms in many patients.
Repeated inflammatory episodes increase cumulative stenotic remodeling and persistent claudication.
IL-6 and IL-1 mediated systemic inflammation often causes fever or fever of unknown origin.
Subacute fever history can be the main presenting feature in occult or large-vessel GCA.
IL-6 drives hepatic CRP synthesis; values are often markedly elevated but can be normal in occult presentations or after treatment.
Fibrinogen, anemia, and immunoglobulin changes raise ESR, though ESR can be modest or normal in some true GCA.
IL-6 mediated thrombopoiesis produces reactive thrombocytosis and contributes to ischemic risk.
Anemia of inflammation is common in systemic GCA and PMR-overlap presentations.
Leukocytosis can accompany systemic inflammation and may mimic infection.
Cytokine activity produces fatigue, malaise, anorexia, and weakness.
Prolonged cytokine activity causes anorexia and weight loss in systemic GCA.
New temporal, frontal, occipital, or diffuse headache is produced by inflamed cranial arteries.
Inflamed superficial scalp arteries produce scalp pain with combing, hats, or palpation.
Temporal artery wall inflammation produces localized tenderness, swelling, erythema, or nodularity.
Temporal artery stenosis or occlusion can produce reduced, absent, thickened, or beaded temporal artery pulses.
Maxillary artery ischemia during chewing produces jaw claudication, a highly specific cranial GCA symptom.
Lingual artery ischemia can produce tongue claudication and rarely tongue necrosis.
Occipital, vertebral, and large-vessel involvement may present with neck pain rather than isolated temporal headache.
Brief retinal or optic nerve hypoperfusion produces amaurosis fugax before permanent visual loss.
Ischemia of ocular motor muscles, nerves, or vertebrobasilar circulation can cause diplopia.
Blurred vision, transient loss, diplopia, or field loss reflect ocular ischemic involvement.
Posterior ciliary, ophthalmic, or retinal artery occlusion can abruptly cause severe permanent vision loss.
Worse visual acuity tracks optic nerve or retinal ischemic injury.
Severe bilateral optic nerve ischemia can cause dilated nonreactive pupils.
Ocular ischemia summarizes ischemic optic neuropathy, retinal artery occlusion, or ophthalmic artery flow compromise.
Active ocular ischemia is the near-term mechanism that makes untreated GCA a vision-threatening emergency.
Aortic wall inflammation is a recognized extracranial GCA manifestation.
Inflamed aortic and branch artery walls become thickened and metabolically active on imaging.
Cumulative intimal hyperplasia produces stenosis in aortic branch vessels.
Subclavian involvement produces arm claudication, bruits, and inter-arm pressure differences.
Axillary artery involvement is common in large-vessel GCA and contributes to upper-limb claudication.
Carotid involvement can produce bruits, cerebral hypoperfusion, and stroke risk.
Vertebral artery involvement is a recognized cause of posterior circulation ischemia in GCA.
Subclavian or axillary stenosis causes exertional arm pain and fatigue.
Iliac or femoral involvement can cause lower-limb claudication in widespread GCA.
Fixed branch stenosis or occlusion produces pulse deficits.
Asymmetric subclavian or axillary stenosis produces inter-arm blood pressure differences.
Turbulent flow across stenotic extracranial arteries produces bruits.
Aortic wall destruction and remodeling expand aneurysm diameter over months to years.
Aortitis-associated aneurysm and medial damage increase dissection risk.
Vertebral, carotid, or intracranial extension of GCA can cause ischemic stroke.
PMR-pattern bursitis and tenosynovitis clinically appear as PMR overlap in many GCA patients.
Subdeltoid bursitis and periarticular inflammation produce shoulder girdle pain and stiffness.
Trochanteric, hip, and pelvic-girdle periarticular inflammation produces hip girdle pain and stiffness.
Inflammatory periarticular pain produces prolonged morning stiffness.
Vision-threatening ischemia marks severe cranial arterial disease and increases overall complication burden, though it is mainly morbidity rather than direct mortality.
Aortic dissection or rupture is a major life-threatening complication of aortitis-associated aneurysm.
GCA-associated stroke increases near-term mortality and disability.
Very high systemic inflammation, anemia, thrombocytosis, and constitutional decline contribute to frailty and complication risk in older adults.
High-dose glucocorticoids, IL-6 blockade, and immunosuppressants increase serious infection risk.
Serious infection in an older immunosuppressed patient raises near-term mortality risk.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Both track systemic acute-phase activity, but either can be normal or discordant.
IL-6 activity drives both CRP and reactive thrombocytosis.
Anemia of inflammation can raise ESR while hemoglobin falls.
Fever and CRP often co-vary with cytokine activity but fever may be absent.
Temporal/scalp artery inflammation often produces both headache and scalp tenderness.
Temporal headache clusters with local temporal artery tenderness when superficial temporal arteries are inflamed.
Jaw claudication marks ischemic cranial arterial involvement and increases concern for ocular ischemic events.
Amaurosis fugax is a direct warning sign for imminent permanent visual loss.
Active ocular ischemia is the immediate causal path to permanent visual loss.
Severe visual loss worsens measured visual acuity.
Aortitis increases future aneurysm growth risk.
Larger aneurysm diameter increases dissection and rupture hazard.
Subclavian or axillary branch stenosis produces arm claudication.
Branch stenosis and occlusion cause reduced or absent pulses.
Carotid stenosis can increase cerebral ischemic risk.
Vertebral involvement is overrepresented in GCA-associated posterior circulation stroke.
Shoulder and hip girdle symptoms often co-vary in PMR-pattern GCA.
PMR activity lengthens inflammatory morning stiffness.
Serious infection is a major treatment-related mortality driver in older GCA patients.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Oral therapy may be slower than pulse intravenous therapy when active ocular ischemia is already present.
Immunosuppression can worsen uncontrolled infection; infectious mimics should be evaluated while vision-threatening GCA is not left untreated.
Diabetes, delirium, psychosis, and frailty raise harm from high-dose steroids.

failure_modes: Persistent fixed stenosis despite inflammatory control
Delayed treatment after completed ocular infarction cannot restore lost vision

side_effects.interpretation: Hyperglycemia risk, especially with diabetes or high steroid dose.
Dose- and duration-dependent serious infection risk.
Higher risk with age, aspirin, anticoagulants, or ulcer history.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid systemic anti-inflammatory treatment for active GCA, especially cranial pain, PMR overlap, fever, ESR/CRP elevation, and prevention of new ischemic events before fixed injury occurs.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Very high near-term ocular ischemic hazard is the setting where very rapid anti-inflammatory effect matters most.
Pulse dosing raises hyperglycemia, delirium, infection, and psychiatric toxicity risk.

failure_modes: Vision already irreversibly lost before therapy
Pulse toxicity in frail older adults

side_effects.interpretation: Short intense immunosuppression plus subsequent oral steroids increases infection risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid suppression of ocular or neurologic ischemic arteritis when visual symptoms, acute vision loss, or very high vision-loss hazard are present.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: IL-6 blockade can worsen infection and blunt CRP/fever signals.
Screening and prophylaxis/treatment context matters before biologic immunosuppression.
Diverticulitis or perforation risk changes safety of IL-6 receptor blockade.

failure_modes: Active infection or uncontrolled latent infection context
CRP and ESR become unreliable activity markers under IL-6 blockade
Persistent fixed stenosis may not reverse

side_effects.interpretation: Serious infection and masked infection signals.
GI perforation risk, especially with diverticulitis history and steroids.

treatments.context_specific_role: IL-6 pathway suppression for reducing relapse and glucocorticoid exposure, especially in relapsing disease, large-vessel activity, or high steroid-toxicity context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Renal impairment greatly increases methotrexate marrow and mucosal toxicity.
Methotrexate can worsen liver injury and fibrosis risk.

failure_modes: Modest effect size for cranial ischemic threat

side_effects.interpretation: Additional infection risk when combined with glucocorticoids.

treatments.context_specific_role: Steroid-sparing immunomodulation for relapsing or steroid-toxicity-limited GCA when immediate organ-threatening ischemia is not the only active problem.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: T-cell costimulation blockade can worsen active infection.

failure_modes: Limited effect size and evidence base compared with glucocorticoids and IL-6 blockade
treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative biologic immunomodulation for selected relapsing or refractory disease when IL-6 blockade or methotrexate is unsuitable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Bleeding risk can outweigh ischemic-risk modification.
Antiplatelet effect is more relevant when thrombotic/ischemic hazard is high.

side_effects.interpretation: GI bleeding risk with age, steroids, anticoagulants, or ulcer history.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct ischemic-risk modification in selected high-risk cranial or cerebrovascular GCA contexts; it is not an anti-arteritis treatment.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active inflammation increases restenosis and peri-procedural complication risk; inflammation control is usually needed around elective procedures.
Life-threatening aortic complication changes intervention urgency.

failure_modes: Does not suppress systemic or cranial inflammatory disease

side_effects.interpretation: Peri-procedural embolic or hypoperfusion risk depending on anatomy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Structural management for severe symptomatic branch stenosis, critical ischemia, or aortic aneurysm/dissection risk after integrating inflammatory activity and anatomy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Higher baseline fracture hazard makes bone protection more outcome-relevant during prolonged glucocorticoids.
GI protection is more relevant when steroids, aspirin, anticoagulants, or ulcer history raise bleeding risk.

failure_modes: Does not treat GCA inflammatory mechanisms
Renal function and calcium/vitamin D context affect bisphosphonate use

side_effects.interpretation: Bisphosphonate selection and dosing depend on renal function rather than directly causing renal disease in most patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Risk mitigation during prolonged glucocorticoid exposure: bone protection, gastric protection when indicated, vaccination planning, and toxicity monitoring.

age_below_50.trajectory_modulation: True GCA is very uncommon below age 50; alternative vasculitis or mimics should have stronger prior unless other evidence is compelling.

age_50_to_69.trajectory_modulation: Compatible age range with lower prior than older adult groups.

age_70_to_89.trajectory_modulation: Peak age range; higher cranial ischemia and treatment-toxicity stakes.

male.trajectory_modulation: Does not exclude GCA; severe ocular and large-vessel cases occur in men.

present.trajectory_modulation: Higher population incidence in Northern European ancestry cohorts.

coupling_modulation.serum_crp__erythrocyte_sedimentation_rat: may show systemic inflammation without cranial symptoms early

treatment_effect_modulation.intravenous_methylprednisolone_pulse: higher acute hyperglycemia and delirium toxicity

treatment_effect_modulation.tocilizumab: infection can be masked and worsened; requires context evaluation
treatment_effect_modulation.methotrexate: infection risk rises when combined with glucocorticoids
treatment_effect_modulation.high_dose_oral_prednisone_or_prednisolon: toxicity increases but organ-threatening GCA may still require immediate treatment

treatment_effect_modulation.tocilizumab: steroid-sparing relapse suppression becomes more relevant
treatment_effect_modulation.vascular_revascularization_or_aneurysm_r: structural role increases when fixed stenosis or aneurysm dominates

supportive_care: Immediate assessment of visual symptoms, diplopia, amaurosis fugax, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, temporal artery abnormalities, and neurologic deficits at presentation and relapse.
Ophthalmology involvement for any acute or transient visual symptom, with documentation of visual acuity, visual fields, pupil response, and fundus findings.
Baseline and follow-up ESR/CRP/platelets/hemoglobin, while recognizing that normal markers do not exclude GCA and IL-6 blockade suppresses CRP/ESR.
Confirmatory testing such as temporal artery ultrasound, temporal artery biopsy, PET/CT, CTA, or MRA should be stored as confirmatory context rather than ordinary ranking observations in case files.
Screen for aortic and branch-vessel involvement when limb claudication, pulse deficit, bruit, blood pressure asymmetry, refractory symptoms, or systemic-only disease suggests extracranial GCA.
Long-term surveillance for thoracic/abdominal aortic aneurysm or dissection in patients with large-vessel involvement or prior aortitis.
Glucocorticoid toxicity mitigation: glucose monitoring, blood pressure monitoring, delirium/psychiatric monitoring, bone protection, fall-risk assessment, and infection vigilance.
Vaccination planning before prolonged immunosuppression when feasible; avoid live vaccines during significant immunosuppression.
Screen for latent tuberculosis and viral hepatitis before biologic therapy; manage reactivation risk before or during immunosuppression.
Pneumocystis prophylaxis consideration during prolonged high-dose glucocorticoids or combined immunosuppression according to local risk practice.
Bone protection during prolonged glucocorticoids: calcium/vitamin D context, DEXA, bisphosphonate or alternative antiresorptive therapy when indicated.
Gastroprotection when aspirin, anticoagulants, ulcer history, or high-dose steroids create meaningful GI bleeding hazard.
Physical therapy and mobility support for PMR-pattern stiffness and steroid-related deconditioning.
Do not rely on symptom improvement alone to infer full vascular healing; fixed stenosis, aortitis, and aneurysm risk may persist.
Coordinate vascular surgery or interventional radiology for critical limb ischemia, severe fixed stenosis, or aneurysm/dissection risk after inflammatory activity and anatomy are assessed.
